increase in meat eating would be predicted to shorten life by promoting chronic
diseases,’ Stanford says. But Stanford's team has found ‘meat-adaptive genes’ that
evolved to counteract such negative effects, and these genes were so successful that
humans actually lived longer. They enabled human evolution to exploit the positive
aspects of meat, like a reduced stomach capacity needed to obtain the required
calories, protein and other nutrients. While some vegetables and fruit also contain
the required protein, they take longer to digest.
C The other leap forward in human dietary evolution was the discovery of fire, and
hence cooking. ‘Cooking brings big benefits,’ says Wrangham. ‘The most important is
it increases the amount of energy obtained from food, Another is that it makes food
softer, hence quicker to eat.’ Wrangham argues that humans could not extract
sufficient protein and energy from a diet of largely raw meat, and therefore cooking
must have become widespread quite early in the evolution of modern humans,
perhaps over one million years ago. Other scientists say there is no firm evidence of
significant use of cooking until recently in evolutionary terms, that is just under
100,000 years ago.

So how do changes in diet actually drive evolution of our genes? Some important
clues have emerged following the recent discovery of a phenomenon called —
‘epigenetic inheritance’, Epigenetics tells us how our genes communicate with the
surrounding environment. Every cell in our bodies contains the same DNA and
therefore the same genes. But in order to develop the multitude of molecules we
need for our various organs, tissues and immune system, some of these genes
become masked by chemical mechanisms during early development. This much has
been known for a long time, but more recently it has become clear that some
epigenetic changes can also be introduced through interactions between our genes
and the environment, especially the food we eat. ‘And a few of these changes can be
passed on to our children in different ways.
Firstly, mothers can affect their unborn child by what they eat during pregnancy and
later through breast-feeding. Secondly, there is evidence that parents can pass on
epigenetic changes that have occurred as a result of what they eat, through their
eggs and sperm. In the case of males, the critical time may be during their ‘slow
growth’ period between the ages of nine and twelve. While this second link may be
more speculative, there are a number of studies suggesting, strangely, that males
with plenty to eat during their slow growth period are more likely to have children
and even grandchildren who suffer from diabetes. The strongest evidence for this”
comes from examination of records from the isolated Swedish village of Overkalix in
the 1800s, linking health to the success of the year's harvest. Analysis of the data
carried out at the Institute of Child Health in London revealed that children whose
fathers’ slow growth period coincided with cool summers resulting in a poor harvest
were more likely to be free of diabetes and less prone to heart disease. Therefore,
what we eat might not only be important to ourselves and our children, but also to
the evolution of the species.
